newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura bond strength may ward off stiff penalty.
newsitem.headline: Nomura bond strength may ward off stiff penalty.

text.p: Japanese authorities are unlikely to punish Nomura Securities Co Ltd in a way that would risk choking off the huge liquidity the brokerage provides to capital markets, market sources say.

Nomura faces a sterner punishment for its latest trading scandal than was meted out for previous infractions, but its key role in the capital markets may make authorities loath to come down too hard, the sources say.

"Crushing Nomura to pieces would be suicidal for Japan's bond market," said a chief bond trader at a major European brokerage, adding that the authorities would have to weigh the likely repercussions when deciding on any appropriate penalty.
Nomura exerts a powerful influence on every business in the yen bond market and is also Japan's top foreign bond seller.

The sources expect Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF), depending on the findings of an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), to order Nomura to halt some or all of its business for up to six months.
This would be a stiff punishment that would take a bite out of Nomura's profits and prestige but would not threaten the stability of the markets.

"Sidelining Nomura in the bond arena could eventually put upward pressure on interest rates as it means bond issuers could not count on its nationwide sales network, which is superior to others by far," said Shin Nagai, money market manager at ABN AMRO Bank NV Tokyo branch.

The SESC is probing Nomura over its March 6 admission that two of its managing directors made discretionary transactions banned under Japanese law and funnelled profits to a corporate client. The client has been linked by Japanese media to "sokaiya" racketeers, who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt annual shareholder meetings.

If its deals are found to violate a commercial code banning payoffs to racketeers, legal action may also be initiated against Nomura on top of any administrative punishment imposed by the financial authorities.

Financial market sources said they expect the MOF penalties against Nomura, particularly on its stock business, to be heavier than those imposed in 1991, when the brokerage was involved in a similar incident involving a favoured client.

Then, Nomura was found to have violated the Securities and Exchange Law through an excessive sales campaign for shares in railway firm Tokyu Corp and was ordered to suspend stock broking and investment research at 79 offices -- about half of its total offices -- for one month.
MOF also ordered Nomura's headquarters and the seven branches most closely involved in the Tokyu share campaign to halt stock broking business for an additional 11 days.
The ministry also put a two-month ban on Nomura's bond underwriting and its auction participation in Japanese government bonds and government-guaranteed bonds.
Market participants speculated that this time, the likely suspension of bond trading would be longer than two months.
Nomura's right to take fresh cash bond and stock positions on behalf of clients is also likely to be suspended, they said.
But its brokers should still be able to tend to their clients' portfolio needs, such as reshuffling bond portfolios and covering futures positions built through Nomura, they said.

These customer operations would be allowed since otherwise Nomura's clients would be left without an intermediary to move or close positions in line with changes in the marketplace such as interest rates and foreign exchange rates, they said.
They said Nomura traders will be banned from making calls to clients even for those portfolio operations, but will be allowed to receive calls made to them from customers.
"As for the stocks business, the authorities will impose harsher penalties than last time to make sure Nomura pays for its scandal," a source close to the brokerage said.

But traders said that while Nomura has the biggest market share in stockbroking, its influence on the share market is less significant than in bonds, making a temporary absence from the market less damaging overall.
Authorities could justify a milder penalty on Nomura's bond business since the suspected illegal deals do not appear to have involved bonds, the source close to the brokerage said.

"In view of Japan's financial market deregulation programme emphasising the 'fairness' of trade, penalties on Nomura should be of the heaviest nature -- but Nomura has become too influential to be punished thoroughly," Nagai said.
